lessons.title: Reading for Main Idea and Evidence

description.text: Find what a passage is mainly doing, then prove an answer from its details.

lessons.subject: use-of-english

objectives.statement: State the main idea of a passage without reducing it to one minor detail.
Match an answer to the sentence or group of details that supports it.

text.text: A passage may mention birds' calls, feeding and predators, but its main idea can be narrower than the list of details. The question is not simply 'What words did I see?' It is 'What point does the writer develop with those details?'

The main idea is the passage's controlling point. A detail may be true but still be too small to represent the whole passage. To find the main idea, read the opening and closing, notice repeated ideas, and ask what the details are doing together. For a factual question, return to the exact sentence; for an inference, combine clues without adding outside knowledge.

items.text: Read once for the situation and writer's subject.
Mark repeated words or related details.
Reduce the passage to one complete sentence.
For each option, ask which sentence proves it and whether it answers the question asked.

prompt.text: A passage says that birds make characteristic calls and that, with practice, a listener can identify species from those calls. What makes identification easy?

steps.expression: question asks for the identifying evidence
steps.description: Do not choose another detail merely because it appears in the passage.
These two details directly answer how identification happens.

steps.expression: answer = their characteristic calls with practice
steps.description: The option is supported by the relevant sentence, while feeding and colour are distractions.

answer.text: The birds' characteristic calls, recognised with practice, make identification easy.

text.text: An option can be true somewhere in the passage and still be wrong for the question. Match the option to the exact demand and its evidence.

points.text: Main idea is the controlling point, not a random detail.
Every answer needs traceable passage evidence.
Do not import facts the writer did not give.

prompt.text: A passage says finches may become separated while looking for insects or seeds on tree branches. Why could they become separated?

content.text: While hunting for insects or seeds on branches
When they become hungry after a flight

feedback.text: The passage directly connects separation with searching for insects or seeds on branches. Predators appear in a different point about alarm calls.

prompt.text: Which statement is a main idea rather than a minor detail?

content.text: One bird called loudly at dawn.
The passage explains how calls help birds communicate and remain connected.
A child looked into a wood.

feedback.text: The broader statement explains what several details are doing together; the other options are isolated details.

hint.text: Choose the option that could cover several details.

summary.text: Read for the writer's point, then prove each answer.

lessons.title: Fiction: Character, Comparison and Writer's Purpose

description.text: Use a narrative's character actions and comparisons to explain what the writer wants the reader to notice.

lessons.subject: use-of-english

objectives.statement: Infer a character's suspicion or attitude from actions and surrounding details.
Explain the effect of a comparison or image in a narrative passage.

text.text: In a narrative, a writer may not state a character's belief directly. The character's questions, silences and reactions can reveal suspicion. A comparison such as 'the harmattan arrived like an uninvited guest' also does more than decorate the sentence: it gives the event a human quality and attitude.

For fiction questions, separate what the character knows from what the character suspects. Then ask why the writer chose a particular image. A comparison usually highlights a quality shared by the two things being compared; it may create mood, explain attitude or make an unfamiliar event easier to imagine.

prompt.text: If the harmattan is compared with an uninvited guest, what quality is being emphasised?

steps.description: An uninvited guest enters a place without being wanted.
The comparison gives the weather an unwelcome, intrusive quality.
The image helps the reader feel the speaker's annoyance rather than merely learn that harmattan arrived.

answer.text: The comparison emphasises the harmattan's unwelcome or intrusive arrival.

content.title: Do not explain the image literally

text.text: The harmattan is not a human guest. Explain the quality the comparison transfers: unwanted arrival, intrusion or lack of welcome.

points.text: Use character behaviour as evidence for implied belief.
Explain what a comparison makes the reader feel or notice.

prompt.text: A character repeatedly asks questions that adults avoid answering. What is the safest inference?

content.text: The character suspects the adults are hiding something.
The character has already proved a crime.

feedback.text: The repeated unanswered questions support suspicion, but they do not prove a crime or justify the stronger claims.

hint.text: Choose the conclusion supported without exaggeration.

prompt.text: A comparison of a storm to a thief mainly suggests that the storm:

feedback.text: The shared quality is unauthorised entry and taking something away; the image creates a threatening effect.

hint.text: Ask what a thief does, not what a storm literally is.

summary.text: Inference must be strong enough to be meaningful but no stronger than the evidence.

description.text: Identify a consonant sound by how it is produced and compare it with the sound in another word.

objectives.statement: Distinguish consonants by place, manner and voicing in common word contrasts.
Choose a word containing the same target consonant sound even when spelling differs.

text.text: The underlined sound in think is /θ/, made with air passing between the tongue and teeth. The letters th do not always make /θ/: this begins with /ð/.

A consonant question tests the sound, not the spelling. Compare whether the vocal cords vibrate, where the sound is made and how air moves. For example, /θ/ in think is voiceless, while /ð/ in this is voiced; measure contains /ʒ/, the sound also heard in the middle of vision.

items.text: Say the underlined word slowly and isolate the target sound.
Ignore the letters and compare the sound at the same position.
Use a minimal pair when possible: think/this, sip/zip, measure/vision.

prompt.text: Which word has the same consonant sound as the underlined sound in measure: pleasure, mission, chair or yes?

steps.description: The middle sound is the voiced sound in vision and pleasure.
Pleasure contains the same /ʒ/ sound despite a different spelling.
Mission, chair and yes contain different consonant sounds.

answer.text: Pleasure has the same /ʒ/ consonant sound as measure.

text.text: The letters th can represent /θ/ or /ð/, and the sound /ʒ/ can have several spellings. Oral questions reward sound comparison, not visual matching.

points.text: Compare the phoneme, not the written letters.
Use voicing and minimal pairs to check your choice.

prompt.text: Which word has the same initial consonant sound as think?

feedback.text: Think and three begin with the voiceless dental fricative /θ/. This and then begin with voiced /ð/.

hint.text: Say the first sound, not the spelling 'th'.

prompt.text: Which word contains the same middle consonant sound as measure?

feedback.text: Measure and vision contain /ʒ/. The other words contain /ʃ/ or /ʃən/ sounds.

hint.text: Think of the sound in the middle of pleasure.

summary.text: Consonant questions compare sounds, not letters.

description.text: Compare the sound at the end of a word and identify which syllable receives the beat.

objectives.statement: Identify a rhyme by comparing the stressed vowel and following sounds.
Locate primary stress in common two- and three-syllable words.

text.text: Bake rhymes with lake, not back. Record can change its stress when it changes from a noun to a verb. English sound questions ask you to hear both the ending pattern and the strong syllable.

Rhyming words share the same stressed vowel and the sounds after it: bake/lake. They do not need the same spelling. Word stress is the syllable that receives greater prominence through length, loudness or pitch. In record as a noun, the first syllable is stressed; as a verb, the second is stressed.

content.alt: How rhyme and stress questions differ.

prompt.text: Which word rhymes with bake: back, lake, bark or book?

steps.description: Hear the stressed vowel and final consonant, not the spelling alone.
Lake shares /eɪk/ with bake; back, bark and book do not.
Choose the word with the same ending sound.

answer.text: Lake rhymes with bake because both end in /eɪk/.

text.text: The worked comparison above is a listening method, not a claim that every option set contains a rhyme. Check the actual sound of each option; words with similar spelling may not rhyme.

points.text: Rhyme depends on sound after the stressed vowel.
Stress depends on the prominent syllable.
Record the noun and record the verb show why word class matters.

feedback.text: Bake and lake share the /eɪk/ ending. Back has /æk/, bark has /ɑːk/ and book has /ʊk/.

hint.text: Say the final sound of each word aloud.

prompt.text: Which word has a different stress pattern from commit, begin and record as a verb?

feedback.text: Commit, begin, allow, arrive and decide stress the second syllable. Table stresses the first syllable.

hint.text: Say each word and tap the stronger syllable.

summary.text: Hear the ending for rhyme and the strong beat for stress.

lessons.title: Emphatic Stress: What the Speaker Corrects

description.text: Use sentence stress to identify which part of a statement the speaker is correcting or contrasting.

lessons.subject: use-of-english

objectives.statement: Explain how changing the stressed word changes the implied contrast.
Choose the response that correctly emphasises the underlined information.

text.text: Ada bought a NEW car. If someone says Ada bought an old car, stressing NEW corrects the age; if someone says Musa bought it, stressing ADA corrects the owner.

Emphatic stress places the strongest beat on the word that carries new, corrected or contrasted information. The sentence stays grammatically identical, but the implied question changes. Ask what the speaker is correcting: the person, action, object, time, place or quality.

prompt.text: They arrived YESTERDAY. Which question is this stress most likely answering?

steps.description: The time word carries the contrast.
The emphasis supplies the time, not the people or action.
Choose the response that corrects the time of arrival.

answer.text: The stress on YESTERDAY answers a question about when they arrived.

text.text: Do not choose an option because it repeats the sentence. Choose the option that supplies the information the stressed word corrects.

points.text: Turn it into the question being answered.
Select the response that supplies that contrast.

prompt.text: In 'Ada bought a NEW car', what does stress on NEW correct?

content.text: The place where it was bought

feedback.text: NEW contrasts with old or used. The stress does not identify Ada, the place or the time.

hint.text: What is the opposite of new?

prompt.text: In 'They arrived YESTERDAY', which question does the stress answer?

feedback.text: Yesterday is a time expression, so it answers when.

hint.text: Classify yesterday: person, place, manner or time?

summary.text: Emphatic stress identifies the information being corrected.
